Infertility

Human infertility studies report pregnancies and changes in sperm measures, but the small randomized trial found no statistically significant difference in pregnancy rates. Uncontrolled series reported live births, while the recent mouse study's sperm-production changes were not significant.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Human infertility studies report pregnancies and changes in sperm measures, but the small randomized trial found no statistically significant difference in pregnancy rates. Uncontrolled series reported live births, while the recent mouse study's sperm-production changes were not significant.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact infertility category contains 12 publications: five human reports, one mouse study, four reviews or systematic reviews, and two editorials. Reviews and editorials summarize or discuss underlying work and are not additional clinical studies. A separate rat study of intrauterine adhesions is adjacent evidence about a specific uterine injury, not a general infertility treatment. A systematic review of male-fertility research also summarizes 14 ex-vivo semen studies; those laboratory experiments do not establish pregnancy or live-birth effects.

Human and clinical evidence

The only randomized clinical trial in the exact category enrolled 30 patients with recurrent implantation failure. Biochemical pregnancy occurred in 46.7% of the PBM group and 33.3% of controls, while clinical pregnancy occurred in 33.3% and 20.0%, respectively. Neither difference was statistically significant (Jafarabadi et al. 2024).

A controlled but nonrandomized embryo-transfer study reported small, nonsignificant differences in clinical pregnancy, implantation, live birth, and miscarriage. A long-running retrospective overview of selected patients reported pregnancies and live births during a period when PBM was used alone or alongside other assisted-reproduction approaches, but the absence of a concurrent comparison makes the rates difficult to attribute to light. A three-person case series reported three full-term births after multiwavelength PBM, while an older 20-man case series found no improvement in four men with azoospermia and increased sperm counts in some men with oligospermia (Hasan et al. 1989). These observations merit accurate reporting but cannot establish efficacy (Tsai et al. 2020; Ohshiro et al. 2012; Phypers et al. 2024).

Animal evidence

One recent mouse study of azoospermia reported increased VASA expression, germ-cell activity, and sperm production after 808-nm treatment, but these changes were not statistically significant. Its reporting was also limited (Tajalli et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The male-fertility systematic review found that all 14 included semen-irradiation studies reporting efficacy showed increased progressive sperm motility. These experiments use isolated semen samples and varied light protocols; they measure laboratory movement, not fertilization, pregnancy, or healthy birth. One included safety study raised concern, so the results should not be generalized into a claim of established sperm-treatment safety (Eghbaldoost et al. 2023).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human protocols ranged from 633-nm red visible light before frozen-embryo transfer to 850-nm near-infrared transabdominal treatment at 900 mW. The retrospective Japanese series used 830-nm near-infrared light at 60 mW, averaging about 21 sessions. The three-case report combined 660-nm red and several near-infrared wavelengths from 810 to 940 nm. Ex-vivo semen experiments used varied wavelengths and doses, while the mouse study reported 808 nm and 4 J/cm². These approaches target different tissues and outcomes, and no study compares a common optimal protocol.

Interpretation

The randomized infertility trial showed numerically higher pregnancy rates but did not establish a statistically significant difference. Uncontrolled reports include pregnancies and live births, while laboratory semen findings concern motility rather than fertility itself. The evidence remains preliminary for both female and male clinical outcomes.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for improving pregnancy or live-birth outcomes with PBM Very low for male fertility outcomes
Publications and records12 exact-category articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Human reports include a 30-person randomized trial with numerically higher pregnancy rates that were not statistically different, alongside uncontrolled pregnancies and sperm-count changes. A long-running retrospective series also reported live births but lacks a concurrent comparison. One mouse study found nonsignificant sperm-production changes. Adequately powered trials with clear eligibility, co-treatments, and live-birth outcomes are needed to establish clinical benefit.
